newsitem.title: USA: U.S. opposes new EU conditions on Turkey.
newsitem.headline: U.S. opposes new EU conditions on Turkey.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday said it opposed European efforts to impose new conditions, such as human rights progress, on Turkey's bid for membership of the European Union.
Washington took this view even though its annual human rights report -- due out on Thursday -- will again criticise Ankara for rights abuses, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.

"It is our position that one needs to look at the full scope of our relationship with Turkey...And on balance, there is a strong case to be made by the United States that Turkey should be more fully integrated into Europe despite the fact that there are problems on human rights," he told reporters.

"The United States would not favour creating any artificial or any new conditions that might prevent Turkey from playing a full role in Europe," he said, adding: "We are in favour of full inclusion by Turkey in western institutions."

Burns spoke after Europe's "big five" powers told Turkey on Wednesday that it had every right to aspire to full membership of the European Union but must make progress on human rights, the Kurdish issue and its disputes with Greece.

Foreign ministers from Britain, France, Germany, Spain and Italy met Turkey's Tansu Ciller in Rome to review ties amid tensions over Cyprus and signals from Ankara it could veto NATO expansion plans if its EU aspirations remain frustrated.

Burns said he had not seen Ciller's remarks about possibly vetoing NATO expansion plans and "cannot believe that she's been quoted correctly" because Turkey is a NATO member and backed a January 1994 decision by NATO leaders to enlarge the alliance.

Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, in her first meeting with foreigners since taking office last week, held talks on Tuesday with Dutch Foreign Minister Hans Van Mierlo, whose country holds the rotating European Union presidency, and European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan.

During the meeting, Albright gave EU officials "a strong sense" of the U.S. view of Turkey "and that is that Turkey is a European country...(and) we need, all of us, to make sure that Turkey is embedded in the major Western institutions. Not only NATO, but in a stronger affiliation with the European Union," Burns said.
Albright told her EU visitors "it's important to send the right signals to Turkey," the spokesman said.
He insisted Albright "did not give any specific advice nor would she on this issue of (EU) membership because that's something for the EU countries alone to decide."
He specifically said Albright did not urge the Europeans to speed up Ankara's acceptance into the EU.
"Now all of us recognise -- and you'll see tomorrow in the publication of our human rights reports -- that there are human rights problems in Turkey," Burns said.

Nevertheless, he said: "There is a strategic rationale for maintaining Turkey's position in Europe. And the United States would not favour creating any artificial or any new conditions that might prevent Turkey from playing a full role in Europe."

In Rome, Ciller stressed Turkey's frustration at what it considers its "second rate" relationship with the 15-nation EU. She signalled that Ankara, a NATO founding member and key strategic ally of the West, could veto plans by the alliance to expand into former communist states unless the EU delivered on closer ties.

At his daily news briefing, Burns did not elaborate on what specific criticisms against Turkey would be in the annual human rights report. But in recent years, the United States has faulted Ankara for its treatment of Kurds.
